topic: How Claude builds a web app — Vox-style 60s vertical Arabic explainer
research_summary: The most important content insight: the existing landscape is saturated with 'look what I built in 10 minutes' tool-demo content, and almost none of it shows the one thing beginners actually ask about — the loop. Claude Code's own documentation frames it as three blending phases (gather context, take action, verify results) repeating until done, with no vector index and no embeddings; it searches with grep and file reads. That loop is the underserved gap and it is inherently animatable: a cycle diagram that spins, a test bar that goes red then green, a file tree that lights up as it is read. The sharpest available tension is the METR randomized trial, where 16 experienced developers were 19% slower with AI yet still believed they were 20% faster — a perfect Vox 'expectation vs reality' two-bar moment. The most promising animation approach is diagram-led motion graphics authored in code (Remotion or HyperFrames) rather than generated footage: the Vox look is built from flat vector type, charts, annotated UI and hard cuts, which is exactly what a code-authored composition does well and which sidesteps this machine having zero image/video generation providers configured. Arabic imposes one hard technique constraint confirmed by independent sources: per-letter animation breaks Arabic glyph joining, so every reveal must be word-level or whole-shape.

data_points.claim: Claude Code works through three blending phases — gather context, take action, verify results — repeating until the task is complete, and the user can interrupt at any point.
data_points.source_name: Claude Code documentation, 'How Claude Code works'
data_points.usable_as: script_anchor — this is the spine of the whole video and the central animated diagram

data_points.claim: Claude Code does not index the codebase: no vector database and no embeddings. It uses file-based agentic search — grep/ripgrep plus file reads — orchestrated by the model.
data_points.source_name: Third-party architecture write-up (corroborated in part by official docs' description of search tools)
data_points.usable_as: stat_card / myth-buster beat — most people assume the model 'has read your whole repo'

data_points.claim: In a METR randomized controlled trial, 16 experienced developers took 19% longer to complete 246 real tasks with AI tools, while still believing afterwards that they had been 20% faster. Beforehand they predicted a 24% speed-up.
data_points.source_name: METR randomized controlled trial, 2025 (summarized by DX)
data_points.usable_as: hook or closing punch — the strongest two-bar 'felt vs measured' chart in the brief

data_points.claim: In the same trial, developers accepted fewer than 44% of AI-generated code, with most saying they had to make major changes to clean it up.
data_points.usable_as: stat_card supporting the 'review is your job' beat

data_points.claim: As of May–July 2026 fieldwork across 15,000+ developers, about 90% used AI coding agents at work at least weekly and about 68% daily.
data_points.source_name: JetBrains Developer Ecosystem / AI agent adoption research 2026
data_points.usable_as: opening context card — establishes 'everyone is already doing this' in one frame

data_points.claim: Per-letter text animation breaks Arabic: letters join and change shape by position, so splitting text into individual glyphs severs those connections before the animation even begins.
data_points.source_name: Framer component author on shape-safe Arabic text animation
data_points.usable_as: production constraint — binds every text reveal in the composition to word-level motion

data_points.claim: Instagram's vertical safe area is widely given as 14% top / 35% bottom / 6% sides — roughly 270px top, 670px bottom and 65px per side on a 1080×1920 frame — though sources disagree and none cite a primary Meta page.
data_points.usable_as: layout constraint — defines where type and charts may live in the frame

data_points.claim: Claude Code snapshots affected files before editing, so edits are reversible independently of git, and 'Plan' mode gates the loop so the agent proposes without touching source files.
data_points.usable_as: reassurance beat — directly answers the 'what if it wrecks my project' fear

misconceptions.myth: The model has read and memorized your entire repository.
misconceptions.reality: It searches the files it needs with grep and reads a handful — there is no index, no vector database, no embeddings.

misconceptions.myth: You describe the app once and it comes out finished.
misconceptions.reality: It is a loop with you inside it. One giant prompt leaves requirements missed; practitioners report the first version is never the final one.

misconceptions.myth: If it compiles and runs, it is done.
misconceptions.reality: A demo is not a production app; auth, data access and security are the easiest things to get silently wrong.

misconceptions.myth: AI assistance always makes an experienced developer faster.
misconceptions.reality: In METR's trial the same developers were 19% slower on familiar codebases while feeling 20% faster.

misconceptions.myth: Writing the code is the hard part, so the agent does the hard part.
misconceptions.reality: Verification is half the loop — running the tests, reading the failure, fixing, running again. That is where the work moved to.

audience_insights.knowledge_level: Arabic-speaking Instagram audience that already knows AI can write code and has probably tried a chat-based tool. Already known: prompting, 'AI writes code', the ten-minutes-to-an-app genre. New to them: that it is a loop rather than a single generation; that search is grep rather than memory; that verification is the agent's own job; that edits are snapshotted and reversible; that the felt speed-up is measurably contested. Assume no familiarity with CLI tooling and no patience for jargon — zero English technical terms unglossed, and the Latin product name 'Claude Code' kept LTR.
pain_points: Builds something that works, then cannot fix it when it breaks
Cannot tell what was decided for them versus what they chose
No mental model for why the agent sometimes takes many steps
Fear of the agent destroying work with no way back
Arabic technical content is scarce, so they learn from English material they only half follow

expert_voices.name: METR (research org)
expert_voices.title_or_affiliation: Ran the randomized controlled trial on AI developer productivity
expert_voices.position: The 19% figure is a 'point-in-time measurement'; the findings do not suggest the tools are useless, only that current tools may fall short in complex environments where developers have deep expertise.

expert_voices.name: Claude Code documentation
expert_voices.position: 'Delegate, don't dictate' — give context and direction and let the agent work out which files to read and which commands to run.

visual_references.description: Vox's choppy, reduced-frame-rate motion — graphics stepped at roughly 12fps against smooth footage, with motion blur deliberately removed from graphics, text and even footage of people to create contrast
visual_references.what_works: The stepped cadence reads as handmade and deliberate rather than templated, and killing motion blur makes type feel stamped onto the frame instead of floating over it. Both are trivially reproducible in a code-authored composition by quantizing the frame used for interpolation.

visual_references.description: Board-based structure: each scene is one visual idea, one narration line, one on-screen label, and the label never repeats the voice
visual_references.what_works: It forces the script and the visuals to carry different information, which doubles the information density without raising the cognitive load. At 60 seconds this is the difference between 12 clear beats and 12 redundant ones. Note: single vendor source with commercial interest — treat as a working heuristic, not as Vox's documented practice.

visual_references.description: The element vocabulary third parties consistently name: clean flat motion graphics, maps, the highlighter/marker sweep, charts, bold typography, and animated archival collage
visual_references.what_works: A small, fixed vocabulary reused across scenes is what makes the style legible as a style. For this brief the maps and archival collage do not apply, which leaves highlighter sweep, charts, bold type and annotated UI — all vector, all authorable in code, none requiring the image/video generation providers this machine lacks.

visual_references.description: Community-reverse-engineered Vox design tokens: saturated yellow primary, near-black ink, 0px border radius (square corners), Balto display / Harriet serif / Roboto Mono eyebrows
visual_references.what_works: Square corners and a single saturated accent against near-black are the load-bearing choices and they translate directly to Arabic type. Important caveat: this is a third-party reading of vox.com, not Vox Media brand material, and nothing in research confirmed 'bold condensed' as official Vox identity — so the palette is an interpretation to approve, not a spec to match.

visual_references.description: Kinetic typography discipline: readable with the sound off, used sparingly alongside icons, with roughly 20% negative space around elements; it fails when motion becomes necessary to understand the words
visual_references.what_works: Directly applicable to a sound-off Instagram feed, and it sets the test for every text beat: freeze any frame and it should still read.

visual_references.description: Arabic-safe motion: animate whole words or connected shapes, never individual glyphs; verify reveal direction under RTL because LTR-built presets such as typewriter run the wrong way
visual_references.what_works: This is the constraint that decides the entire text-animation system for this video, and it matches the rule already enforced in the user's tasmeem project (split on spaces only, no letterSpacing).

angles_discovered.name: The loop you never see
angles_discovered.hook: You typed one sentence. It made forty decisions — here is the loop it ran while you waited.
angles_discovered.why_now: This is the brief's clearest underserved gap: the official documentation defines the agentic loop as gather context, take action, verify results, repeating until done, yet none of the five landscape entries animates it. Animation fit: diagram-led motion graphics — a three-node cycle that physically spins, with the file tree lighting up on 'gather', a diff stamping in on 'act', and a test bar flipping red to green on 'verify'. Maps to code-authored vector motion (Remotion or HyperFrames), which the technique research confirms is a proven pairing for Vox styling and which needs none of the generation providers this machine lacks.
grounded_in: data_point: three blending phases, repeating until complete (primary, Claude Code docs)
data_point: snapshots before editing and Plan mode gating
audience_question: 'Why does it take so many steps?'
misconception: 'you describe it once and it comes out finished'
underserved_gap: nobody animates the loop; verification half never shown

angles_discovered.name: It doesn't know your code — it looks
angles_discovered.hook: It never read your project. It greps for the four files it needs, like you would.
angles_discovered.why_now: The single most load-bearing misconception in the audience research, and the one that explains both the agent's strengths and its blind spots. Reported in text by one secondary source and corroborated by the official docs' description of search tooling, but visualized nowhere. Animation fit: annotated-UI plus highlighter sweep — a file tree where a grep query sweeps through and four files illuminate while hundreds stay dark, then those four expand into the context window as a filling bar. This is the Vox highlighter-marker vocabulary applied to a code tree instead of a map, and it is pure vector work.
grounded_in: data_point: no vector database, no embeddings, grep plus file reads
misconception: 'the model has memorized your repo'
audience_question: 'Does it actually read my whole project, or is it guessing?'
pain_point: no mental model for the agent's behaviour

angles_discovered.name: Felt faster, measured slower
angles_discovered.hook: Sixteen experienced developers felt 20% faster. The stopwatch said 19% slower.
angles_discovered.why_now: The strongest single number in the brief and the only genuinely counterintuitive one, from a randomized controlled trial rather than a vendor survey — against a 2026 backdrop where ~90% of developers already use these agents weekly, so the audience has a felt experience to contradict. Animation fit: chart-led motion graphics — two bars racing from a shared baseline, the 'felt' bar overshooting while the 'measured' bar sinks below the line, held long enough to land. Stat-card and chart work, the most mechanically reliable thing to author in code and the most legible beat in a vertical frame.
grounded_in: data_point: METR 19% slower, 20% believed faster, 24% predicted
data_point: fewer than 44% of AI code accepted without major changes
audience_question: 'Is it actually faster, or does it just feel faster?'

angles_discovered.name: What it decided while you weren't looking
angles_discovered.hook: 'Add a login.' It picked your database, your session rules and where your secrets live.
angles_discovered.why_now: This is the audience's actual lived pain — the research repeatedly surfaces hidden decisions and the later crash as the beginner's defining experience — and it has a natural narrative shape: one short prompt, then an unfolding stack of consequences. Animation fit: kinetic typography plus progressive diagram build — one Arabic line of prompt at the top, then silent decision chips stacking beneath it one by one until they overflow the frame. Word-level Arabic reveals only, which satisfies the glyph-joining constraint while still giving the stepped Vox cadence.
grounded_in: misconception: 'if it compiles and runs, it is done'
audience_question: 'What is it deciding for me that I never see?'
pain_point: 'works, then breaks, and I cannot tell what changed'
